items.prose: An insurer sells a year of phone cover for £60. Over the year, a policy's claim $X$ is £0 with chance 0.85, £200 with chance 0.1 and £500 with chance 0.05.

parts.question: What is the expected claim $E[X]$, in pounds? Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply each claim by its chance, then add.

byKey.unweighted: You averaged the three claims equally. Most policies claim nothing, so weight each claim by its chance.
byKey.missed-500: You left out the £500 claim. It adds $500 \times 0.05 = 25$.
byKey.mode: That is the most likely claim. The expected claim weights every value by its chance.

explain.text: The expected value is the probability-weighted average of the claims. The £0 claims add nothing, so $E[X] = 20 + 25 = 45$ pounds.

parts.question: Using $E[X] = £45$, what is the insurer's expected profit on one policy, in pounds? Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.correct: Expected profit is the price minus the expected claim: $60 - 45 = 15$, so £15.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The insurer takes the £60 and pays out the claim.

byKey.reversed: That is the buyer's side. The insurer receives £60 and expects to pay £45.
byKey.carried-unweighted: You used £233.33, part 1's unweighted average. With $E[X] = 45$ the profit is £15.
byKey.carried-500: You used £20, part 1's slip without the £500 claim. With $E[X] = 45$ the profit is £15.

explain.text: The insurer's profit is $60 - X$. Its expected value is $60 - E[X] = 60 - 45 = 15$ pounds.

parts.question: It sells 2,000 policies. A storm can make many claims come together. Using £15 per policy from part 2, what is the expected total profit, in pounds? Give your answer to the nearest pound.

feedback.correct: Expected values add whatever the link: $2000 \times 15 = 30{,}000$, so £30,000.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the expected profit of every policy.

byKey.one-policy: That is one policy. The expected total adds 2,000 of them.
byKey.revenue: That is the premium taken in. Take off the expected claims, $2000 \times 45$.
byKey.claims: That is the expected total paid out. The question asks for profit.

explain.text: Linearity gives $E[\text{total}] = \sum E[\text{profit}_k]$ even when claims are linked. So the total is $2000 \times 15 = 30{,}000$ pounds.

parts.question: The insurer adds a £50 excess: each claim now pays £50 less, so claims are £0, £150 or £450 with the same chances. Using $E[X] = £45$, what price gives an expected profit of £20 a policy? Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.correct: The new claim is $X - 50$ only when a claim is made, chance 0.15: $45 - 50 \times 0.15 = 37.5$, and $37.5 + 20 = 57.5$, so £57.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The £50 comes off only when there is a claim. Find the new expected claim, then add £20.

byKey.excess-all: You took £50 off every policy, as $E[X] - 50 = -5$. Policies with no claim pay £0, not $-$£50.
byKey.old-claims: You kept the old expected claim of £45. The excess lowers it to £37.50.
byKey.fair: That is the new expected claim, the fair price with no profit. Add the £20.

explain.text: The new claim is $X - 50I$, where $I$ marks a claim, with $E[I] = 0.15$. So $E[X - 50I] = 45 - 7.5 = 37.5$, and the price is $37.5 + 20 = 57.50$ pounds.

items.prose: A share rises on a trading day with chance 0.6 and falls otherwise, independently from day to day. Over 20 trading days, a reversal is a day whose move differs from the day before, so day 1 is never one. Let $R$ count the reversals.

parts.question: What is the chance that a given day from day 2 to day 20 is a reversal? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Up then down, or down then up: $0.6 \times 0.4 + 0.4 \times 0.6 = 0.48$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A reversal is up then down, or down then up.

byKey.one-way: That is up then down only. Down then up is a reversal too.
byKey.same: That is the chance of the same move twice. A reversal needs the moves to differ.
byKey.half: You treated up and down as equally likely. Up has chance 0.6.

explain.text: Day $k$ reverses when days $k - 1$ and $k$ move differently. That is $0.6 \times 0.4 + 0.4 \times 0.6 = 0.48$.

parts.question: Let $I_k = 1$ when day $k$ is a reversal. Using $P(I_k = 1) = 0.48$, what is $E[R]$? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Sum the expected values of the indicators. Count which days can reverse.

byKey.twenty: You used 20 days. Day 1 has no day before it, so only 19 days can reverse.
byKey.one-way: You used 0.24, part 1's one-way slip. With 0.48 the answer is $19 \times 0.48$.
byKey.same: You used 0.52, the chance of the same move. With 0.48 the answer is 9.12.

explain.text: Each indicator has $E[I_k] = P(I_k = 1) = 0.48$. By linearity, $E[R] = 19 \times 0.48 = 9.12$.

parts.question: $I_2$ and $I_3$ both depend on day 2's move, so the indicators are not independent. What does that do to $E[R] = 9.12$?

options.text: Nothing: linearity holds for dependent indicators
It lowers it: shared days make reversals cancel out
options.why: Expected values add whatever the link. Dependence changes the spread of $R$, not its mean.

options.text: $E[R]$ cannot be found without the joint distribution
options.why: Linearity needs only each $E[I_k]$, never the joint table.

options.text: It raises it: one reversal makes the next more likely
options.why: Each $P(I_k = 1)$ is still 0.48, and the sum of the means is still 9.12.

feedback.correct: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, so $E[R] = 9.12$ stands.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what linearity of expectation needs.

explain.text: $E[I_2 + \dots + I_{20}] = E[I_2] + \dots + E[I_{20}]$ holds for any random variables. Dependence would matter for the variance, not the mean.

parts.question: A rule loses £5 on each reversal and gains £3 on each other day from 2 to 20. Its P&L is $3(19 - R) - 5R = 57 - 8R$. Using $E[R] = 9.12$, what is its expected P&L, in pounds? Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $E[aR + b] = aE[R] + b$.

byKey.twenty: You counted 20 days of gains. Only days 2 to 20 trade, so 19 days in all.
byKey.no-gains: That is the reversal losses alone, $-5 \times 9.12$. Add the £3 gains on the other days.
byKey.carried: You used 9.6 reversals, part 2's 20-day slip. With $E[R] = 9.12$ the answer is $-15.96$.

explain.text: The P&L is a linear function of $R$. So its expected value is $57 - 8E[R] = 57 - 72.96 = -15.96$ pounds.

parts.question: How much must the rule gain on each non-reversal day for its expected P&L to be zero? Use $E[R] = 9.12$, so $E[19 - R] = 9.88$. Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set the expected gains equal to the expected losses.

byKey.flipped: You divided 9.88 by 9.12. The gains cover $5 \times 9.12$, spread over 9.88 days.
byKey.equal: You set the gain equal to the loss. There are fewer reversal days than other days, 9.12 against 9.88.

explain.text: Expected P&L is $g \times 9.88 - 5 \times 9.12$. It is zero when $g = 45.6 / 9.88 \approx 4.62$ pounds, the fair gain.

items.prose: A share trades at £40. In a month it will close at $S$ = £34, £38, £42 or £48, with chances 0.1, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.2. A call struck at £40 pays $C = \max(S - 40, 0)$, and a put struck at £40 pays $Q = \max(40 - S, 0)$.

parts.question: What is $E[S]$, in pounds? Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight each close by its chance and add.

byKey.unweighted: You averaged the four closes equally. They have different chances.
byKey.mode: That is the most likely close. The expected value weights all four.

explain.text: Each close is multiplied by its chance and the products are added. That gives $E[S] = 41.2$ pounds.

parts.question: What is the call's fair price, $E[C]$, in pounds? Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the payoff at each close, then weight by the chances.

byKey.mean-payoff: That is $\max(E[S] - 40, 0)$. A max is not linear, so take the payoff at each close first.
byKey.top-only: You counted only the £48 close. The £42 close pays £2 as well.
byKey.unweighted: You averaged the payoffs 0, 0, 2 and 8 equally. Weight each by its chance.

explain.text: The payoffs are 0, 0, 2 and 8. Weighting by the chances gives $E[C] = 0.8 + 1.6 = 2.4$ pounds.

parts.question: At every close, $C - Q = S - 40$. Using linearity with $E[S] = 41.2$ and $E[C] = 2.4$, what is the put's fair price, $E[Q]$? Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take expected values of both sides of $C - Q = S - 40$.

byKey.sign: You added 1.2 to the call price. $E[Q] = E[C] - (E[S] - 40)$.
byKey.carried: You used $E[S] = 40.5$, part 1's unweighted slip. With 41.2 the put is worth 1.2.

explain.text: Linearity gives $E[C] - E[Q] = E[S] - 40 = 1.2$, so $E[Q] = 1.2$ pounds. Check: the put pays £6 at £34 and £2 at £38, and $0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2$.

parts.question: A dealer sells the call for £2.10 and buys the put for £1.50. A trader buys the call and sells the put to him at those prices. Using $E[C] = 2.4$ and $E[Q] = 1.2$, what is her expected profit, in pounds? Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the expected profit of each leg: bought legs gain payoff minus price, sold legs price minus payoff.

byKey.both-bought: You treated the put as bought. She sells it, so she gains £1.50 and expects to pay £1.20.
byKey.call-only: That is the call leg only. Selling the put at £1.50 adds £0.30.
byKey.sign: You took the dealer's side. She pays £2.10 for a call worth £2.40.

explain.text: Profit is $(C - 2.10) + (1.50 - Q)$. By linearity its expected value is $0.30 + 0.30 = 0.60$ pounds.

items.prose: A bag holds 10 tokens: 3 gold, worth £20 each, and 7 silver, worth £5 each. A player draws 4 tokens without replacement and keeps their value. Let $G$ be the number of gold tokens drawn.

parts.question: What is the chance that the third token drawn is gold? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Every position is equally likely to hold any token, so the chance is $\tfrac{3}{10} = 0.3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Before any token is seen, the third draw is as likely to be gold as the first.

byKey.shrunk: You took $\tfrac{3}{8}$, as if two silver tokens were gone. Nothing is known about the first two draws.
byKey.summed: You added the chance over three draws. The question is about the third draw alone.

explain.text: Unseen draws are symmetric: the third token is a random one of the 10. So it is gold with chance $\tfrac{3}{10}$.

parts.question: Let $I_k = 1$ when draw $k$ is gold, so $G = I_1 + I_2 + I_3 + I_4$. Using $E[I_k] = 0.3$, what is $E[G]$? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: $E[G] = 4 \times 0.3 = 1.2$. The draws are dependent, but linearity does not care.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the four expected indicators.

byKey.one-draw: That is one draw. $G$ adds four indicators.
byKey.all-gold: That is the number of gold tokens in the bag. Only 4 of the 10 tokens are drawn.
byKey.shrinking: You used $\tfrac{3}{10} + \tfrac{3}{9} + \tfrac{3}{8} + \tfrac{3}{7}$, as if every draw before was silver. Each draw is gold with chance 0.3.

explain.text: Each $E[I_k] = 0.3$, so $E[G] = 1.2$. Linearity holds even though the draws are without replacement.

parts.question: The value drawn is $V = 20G + 5(4 - G) = 20 + 15G$ pounds. Using $E[G] = 1.2$, what is $E[V]$? Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $E[a + bG] = a + bE[G]$.

byKey.no-silver: You counted only the gold, $20 \times 1.2$. The silver tokens add £5 each.
byKey.mean-token: You gave each token the plain average of £20 and £5. Silver is more common.
byKey.drop-shift: You left out the 20 in $20 + 15G$. Every draw of 4 is worth at least £20.
byKey.carried: You used 1.437, part 2's shrinking slip. With $E[G] = 1.2$ the answer is £38.

explain.text: Linearity gives $E[20 + 15G] = 20 + 15E[G] = 20 + 18 = 38$ pounds. Check: each draw is worth $0.3 \times 20 + 0.7 \times 5 = 9.5$ on average, and $4 \times 9.5 = 38$.

parts.question: The game adds a £15 bonus for the second gold token drawn and a further £15 for the third. What is $P(G \ge 2)$? Give a fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the 4-token hands with 2 or 3 gold among the $\binom{10}{4} = 210$.

byKey.replaced: You used the binomial with chance 0.3, as if tokens went back. They do not, so count hands.
byKey.exactly-two: That is $G = 2$ alone. A hand with all 3 gold also earns the bonus.
byKey.at-least-one: That is $P(G \ge 1)$. The bonus needs 2 gold tokens.

explain.text: There are 210 hands of 4. Two gold and two silver gives $3 \times 21 = 63$, and three gold gives 7, so $P(G \ge 2) = \tfrac{70}{210} = \tfrac{1}{3}$.

parts.question: Using $E[V] = £38$, $P(G \ge 2) = \tfrac{1}{3}$ and the 7 hands with three gold tokens, what is the fair price to play, in pounds? The bonus is £15 for each gold token after the first. Give your answer to the nearest penny.

feedback.correct: The bonus is $15\,(J_2 + J_3)$, where $J_2$ marks $G \ge 2$ and $J_3$ marks $G = 3$. So the fair price is $38 + 15 \times (\tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{30}) = 43.50$ pounds.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The fair price is the expected payout: the tokens plus the expected bonus.

byKey.no-bonus: That is the tokens alone. Add the expected bonus.
byKey.once-only: You paid £15 once, for $G \ge 2$. A third gold token earns a further £15, with chance $\tfrac{1}{30}$.
byKey.full-bonus: You added the whole £15. The bonus is paid only some of the time.
byKey.bonus-only: That is the expected bonus alone. Add the £38 of tokens.
byKey.carried: You used the with-replacement chances 0.3483 and 0.0837. Counting hands gives $\tfrac{1}{3}$ and $\tfrac{1}{30}$, so the price is £43.50.
byKey.carried-half: You used 0.3483, the with-replacement chance, for $G \ge 2$. Counting hands gives $\tfrac{1}{3}$, so the price is £43.50.

explain.text: A bonus of £15 for each token after the first is $15(G - 1)$ when $G \ge 1$, and $G \ge 2$ pays £15 and $G = 3$ a second £15. Three gold has chance $\tfrac{7}{210} = \tfrac{1}{30}$, so the expected bonus is $15 \times (\tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{30}) = 5.50$ pounds. Adding it to $E[V]$ gives a fair price of $38 + 5.50 = 43.50$ pounds.
